recorded-direction.text: The diagram draws design direction, executable model, reviewed contract and production implementation vertically as distinct stages. The later stages remain unproved. Decisions preserve own-anchor independence, institutional publication as an explicit trust option, and availability purchased separately from authority.

named-deployment-roles.text: Anchors and ledgers run nodes. Anchors serve signed roots; ledgers serve data and proofs. Applications serve application proofs. Terminals consume all three, verify them and build transactions or drive real-world effects. The names describe roles rather than a fixed deployment count.

words-that-constrain-the-design.text: The rulings require immutable content separate from chainpoint indexes, independent per-block anchor publication and an API governed by coherent evidence rather than Koios compatibility. Historical CBOR can be untrusted reconstruction material. The preserved present-validity and future-validation ruling distinguishes off-chain ledger membership checks from application proofs used in redeemers.

claims-and-evidence-boundaries.text: This table separates architecture from delivery. Lockness has no accepted formal model, verifier or end-to-end deployment. Own and institutional anchors express trust choices, not measured price rankings; no institution is claimed to participate today. CSMT machinery exists, but archive, sessions and application replay need further work. Membership alone proves neither uniqueness nor settlement.

what-remains-unproved.text: Open contracts cover anchor costs, interoperability, proof scopes, completeness, archive coverage and references, anchor policies, retained views, unique state assumptions and exact application bindings. Irreversible effects also need settlement evidence. Coverage must be selected before cost commitments.

evidence-available-today.text: MPFS already verifies reconstructed facts against an anchored state root. The inspected Koios and Blockfrost interfaces do not promise the required shared chainpoint sessions. Related root-signing work is not evidence that the whole publication protocol exists.
